strengths: Auditing classifiers from aggregate label proportions addresses an important problem when individual validation data are unavailable. The formulation usefully distinguishes classifier properties from what limited observations can establish.

The shared-baseline mixture model gives unfairness a precise mathematical interpretation. Monotonicity under label coarsening and the finite candidate characterization for known binary confusion matrices are useful structural results.

The multiclass computational methods provide a meaningful extension of the acknowledged 2020 binary work. Greedy initialization followed by local optimization substantially improves the reported upper bounds, sometimes matching the lower bound.

The experiments cover over 800 binary classifiers and several multiclass applications. Reporting loose bounds on Adult and COMPAS helps clarify limitations. Detailed derivations and links to implementation and experiment code support reproducibility.
weaknesses: Lemma 4 is false as stated, undermining the supplied justification for Algorithm 2's tolerance guarantee. Set a=c=0, b=1, d=1/2, and beta=1/2. For x in (0,1), its function is psi(x)=3/4-x/4, whose derivative has magnitude 1/4, whereas the stated bound is zero. Appendix B bounds the derivative of eta but omits the varying error contribution in tau_beta. The lemma, search resolution, and resulting numerical guarantees require correction and validation.

The written discrepancy objectives contain consequential inconsistencies. Section 8.1 switches to false-positive/false-negative rates while retaining tau_beta(a,b)=beta*eta(a,b)+(1-beta)*(1-b), reversing the intended error contribution. In Equations (29) and (32), the error term also lacks the population weights w_g*pi_g^y: F^y is defined using ones rather than these weights. These corrections are algebraically straightforward, but the manuscript must establish that the implementation and results optimize the intended objective.

Sections 8 and 8.3 claim that varying beta recovers tight constrained fairness/error optima and the full Pareto trade-off. Weighted-sum minimization provides supporting bounds, but recovering all constrained optima requires additional conditions. No convexity or strong-duality argument is established for this nonconvex unfairness measure. Consequently, the exact constrained conclusions used in the cancer examples are insufficiently justified.

The advertised advantage for rare labels is overstated. Equation (6) weights deviations by class prevalence, so disparities confined to a rare true class contribute at most that class's probability. Moreover, choosing the identity matrix as baseline shows unfairness <= error. Thus severe conditional disparities can receive arbitrarily small values, contrary to Section 6.1's claim that doubling misdiagnosis rates for a rare disease necessarily manifests as high unfairness. The prevalence normalization used in the experiments needs to be reconciled with these claims.

Validation of the new multiclass aggregate method is incomplete. Tables 9–12 report local upper bounds on mindisc_1 without corresponding certified lower bounds or optimization gaps for the same aggregate inputs. These upper bounds characterize limitations of auditability; large values cannot certify unavoidable unfairness. Interpreting the election curve as variation in the minimum therefore requires stronger optimization evidence. Multiclass trade-offs with beta<1 and runtime comparisons supporting the new fast binary solver are also missing.

The applications require all aggregate inputs to describe the same population and compatible time periods. Combining Bing-user self-reports with general-population cancer incidence does not establish this alignment. Although Section 5 mentions uncertainty margins, the application analyses do not propagate sampling uncertainty or examine population mismatch. The resulting fairness conclusions therefore depend on substantial unvalidated assumptions.
